    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

            - '\rundll32.exe'

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Microsoft Maps Three Salesforce Attack Paths Tied to a Year of ShinyHunters Activity

The Hacker News
2026-07-14 10 use cases 4 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Attackers whose methods line up with the data-extortion group&nbsp;ShinyHunters&nbsp;have spent the past year walking into corporate Salesforce environments without exploiting a single flaw in the platform. The way in has been the trust the organization had already extended, usually through the OAuth connections that tie Salesforce to the apps and third-party vendors around it. In&nbsp;

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Salesforce consent to spoofed 'Data Loader' connected app (UNC6040 vishing) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated Salesforce Aura/GraphQL guest scraping past 2,000-record limit · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Compromised vendor OAuth integration (Drift/Gainsight/Klue) mass Salesforce export · [LLM] Salesforce SOQL secret-hunting across Case/support objects (AWS/Snowflake/VPN) · [LLM] Anti-forensic deletion of Salesforce async query/bulk job records · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Salesforce consent to spoofed 'Data Loader' connected app (UNC6040 vishing) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts OAuth consent grants inside Salesforce to a connected app branded as 'Data Loader' but not the legitimate Salesforce client, the payoff of the ShinyHunters/UNC6040 vishing calls. Surfaces the granting user, source IP and geo so an analyst can confirm the call/consent chain. Rationale: Keys on the article's explicit lure — a connected app 'dressed up as Salesforce's own Data Loader tool' — corroborated by GTIG/Mandiant which note the consented app's name/branding differs from the legit Data Loader. Consent event ties the malicious app to a specific user identity, IP and geo. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2025/250912.pdf • https://appomni.com/blog/detecting-unc6040-vishing-in-salesforce-oauth-attacks/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1078.004 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately installing/authorizing the genuine Salesforce Data Loader connected app for data migration
  • Data migration or ETL project onboarding a Data Loader-style integration
  • Sandbox refresh where connected apps are re-consented
  • Third-party MSP performing an authorized bulk data load
  • Renamed internal integration that happens to contain 'Data Loader' in its label
Suppression filter
| where not (ConsentedApp has "Data Loader" and IsAdminOperation == true and CountryCode in ("US","GB"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the consenting user and confirm out-of-band whether they authorized a Data Loader app in the last 24h; check if the client_id matches Salesforce's official Data Loader vs an arbitrary/attacker app id and whether a vishing call preceded it. 2) Contain: in Salesforce Setup > Connected Apps OAuth Usage, revoke the app's tokens and block the app; force re-auth / reset the user's session. 3) Hunt: review that app's ApiEvent/BulkApi activity for enumeration and secret-hunting SOQL, and check for other users who consented to the same app id.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Consent","Connected","OAuth","Authorize","Grant")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend ConsentedApp = coalesce(tostring(Raw.ConnectedApplication), tostring(Raw.ConnectedAppName), ObjectName)
| where ConsentedApp has "Data Loader"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, ActionType, ConsentedApp, ObjectId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Consent","Connected","OAuth","Authorize","Grant")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend ConsentedApp = coalesce(tostring(Raw.ConnectedApplication), tostring(Raw.ConnectedAppName), ObjectName)
| where ConsentedApp has "Data Loader"
| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, ActionType, ConsentedApp, ObjectId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

level: medium
APPLICATION

| search APP_NAME="*Data Loader*" OR CONNECTED_APP_NAME="*Data Loader*" OR OBJECT_NAME="*Data Loader*"

Compromised vendor OAuth integration (Drift/Gainsight/Klue) mass Salesforce export AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts high-volume SOQL/Bulk-API data pulls performed by trusted vendor connected apps named Drift, Gainsight or Klue — the integrations whose stolen OAuth/refresh tokens ShinyHunters (UNC6395/Storm-3138) turned against downstream Salesforce orgs. Flags export volume far above a normal integration sync. Rationale: Names the exact compromised vendor apps from the article (Salesloft Drift, Gainsight, Klue) and thresholds on export volume — the Drift token theth alone reportedly exposed 700+ orgs by querying/exporting Salesforce objects, so bulk row counts by these apps are high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.illumio.com/blog/the-master-key-problem-what-the-salesloft-breach-reveals-about-an-ongoing-threat
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1530 T1567
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate scheduled Gainsight/Drift sync ingesting large object volumes after a new deployment
  • Initial full-history backfill when a vendor integration is first connected
  • Analytics/BI vendor app running a large nightly report export
  • Data migration event temporarily spiking a vendor app's query volume
  • Sandbox seeding where a vendor app bulk-reads production data
Suppression filter
| where not (AppName has_any ("Drift","Gainsight","Klue") and SrcIps has_any ("<known-vendor-egress-range>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the connected app and compare the query volume and source IP/ASN to its 30-day baseline; confirm whether the vendor has disclosed a token-theft incident (Salesloft/Gainsight/Klue advisories). 2) Contain: revoke the app's OAuth/refresh tokens in Salesforce Connected Apps OAuth Usage and disable the integration user; rotate any credentials the exported objects could contain. 3) Hunt: pivot to the SOQL bodies for secret-hunting patterns (AWS/Snowflake), and check for query-job deletions the actor uses to cover tracks.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Api","Bulk","Report","Export","Query")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend AppName = coalesce(tostring(Raw.ConnectedApplication), tostring(Raw.ClientName))
| where AppName has_any ("Drift","Gainsight","Klue")
| extend Rows = toint(coalesce(Raw.RowsProcessed, Raw.NumberOfRecords, Raw.RowCount))
| summarize TotalRows = sum(Rows), Queries = count(), SrcIps = make_set(IPAddress, 15), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AppName, AccountDisplayName
| where TotalRows > 50000 or Queries > 500   // 50k rows / 500 calls = well above a normal chat/CI integration sync cadence
| order by TotalRows desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Api","Bulk","Report","Export","Query")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend AppName = coalesce(tostring(Raw.ConnectedApplication), tostring(Raw.ClientName))
| where AppName has_any ("Drift","Gainsight","Klue")
| extend Rows = toint(coalesce(Raw.RowsProcessed, Raw.NumberOfRecords, Raw.RowCount))
| summarize TotalRows = sum(Rows), Queries = count(), SrcIps = make_set(IPAddress, 15), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AppName, AccountDisplayName
| where TotalRows > 50000 or Queries > 500   // 50k rows / 500 calls = well above a normal chat/CI integration sync cadence
| order by TotalRows desc
APPLICATION
sourcetype=sfdc:* (EVENT_TYPE="ApiEvent" OR EVENT_TYPE="BulkApiResultEvent" OR EVENT_TYPE="ReportExportEvent") 
| search CONNECTED_APP_NAME IN ("*Drift*","*Gainsight*","*Klue*") OR APP_NAME IN ("*Drift*","*Gainsight*","*Klue*") 
| eval rows=coalesce(ROWS_PROCESSED,NUMBER_OF_RECORDS,ROW_COUNT,0) 
| stats sum(rows) as totalRows count as queries dc(SOURCE_IP) as srcIPs values(SOURCE_IP) as src min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by CONNECTED_APP_NAME, USER_NAME 
| where totalRows > 50000 OR queries > 500 
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) 
| sort - totalRows
Salesforce SOQL secret-hunting across Case/support objects (AWS/Snowflake/VPN) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts SOQL/API queries whose body searches Salesforce records (support cases, notes) for embedded secrets — AWS access keys, Snowflake tokens, VPN and password strings — exactly the loot UNC6395 sifted for after stealing Drift tokens. Content match on the AKIA prefix and secret keywords. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit statement that operators ran SOQL to sift support cases for AWS keys, Snowflake tokens and passwords; the AWS 'AKIA' access-key prefix plus 'snowflakecomputing' are low-FP content anchors that ordinary CRM queries rarely contain. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://www.illumio.com/blog/the-master-key-problem-what-the-salesloft-breach-reveals-about-an-ongoing-threat
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1213 T1530
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running a legitimate secret-sprawl audit across Salesforce records
  • DLP or CASB vendor scanning case bodies for exposed credentials
  • Support agent legitimately searching a case containing the word 'password'
  • Integration that indexes case text for search and echoes keywords in query logs
  • Pentest/red-team engagement authorized to hunt for embedded secrets
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName has_any ("dlp","casb","secaudit") or IsAdminOperation == true)
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the full SOQL body and the querying identity/app — confirm whether the actor is a vendor integration token (see Drift/Gainsight/Klue) or an interactive session, and whether results returned rows. 2) Contain: revoke the querying app/user tokens and immediately rotate any AWS keys, Snowflake tokens or VPN creds that were stored in the matched objects. 3) Hunt: enumerate all objects returned, check for downstream use of the harvested keys in AWS CloudTrail/Snowflake login history, and look for query-job deletion covering the activity.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Api","Query","Report","Bulk")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend Soql = tostring(coalesce(Raw.Query, Raw.QueryString, Raw.Soql))
| where Soql has_any ("AKIA","aws_secret","aws_access","snowflakecomputing","snowflake","vpn","password","passwd","private_key","apikey","api_key","secret")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, ActionType, Soql
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Api","Query","Report","Bulk")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend Soql = tostring(coalesce(Raw.Query, Raw.QueryString, Raw.Soql))
| where Soql has_any ("AKIA","aws_secret","aws_access","snowflakecomputing","snowflake","vpn","password","passwd","private_key","apikey","api_key","secret")
| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, ActionType, Soql

Anti-forensic deletion of Salesforce async query/bulk job records AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts deletion/abort of Salesforce async query, Apex and Bulk-API job records — the track-covering step the Salesloft Drift operators used, deleting their query jobs to slow investigators. Keys on delete/abort actions targeting job objects rather than a bare column. Rationale: Directly targets the article's stated anti-forensic behaviour ('deleting their query jobs to slow down anyone investigating'); scopes to async/bulk job object types so it fires on evidence removal, not routine record deletes. Fixes prior schema error by matching on ActionType values instead of a non-existent 'Delete' column. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion
ATT&CKT1070 T1070.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin housekeeping that clears completed/failed async Apex jobs
  • Bulk-API integration aborting a stuck or duplicate job
  • Scheduled cleanup script pruning old BackgroundOperation records
  • DevOps pipeline aborting bulk loads during a failed deployment
  • Salesforce support aborting a runaway job during a case
Suppression filter
| where not (IsAdminOperation == true and AccountDisplayName has_any ("integration","svc","automation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify who deleted/aborted the job and whether the same identity ran large SOQL/Bulk exports just before the deletion (correlate on user/app + preceding 1h). 2) Contain: preserve remaining Real-Time Event Monitoring logs, revoke the identity's tokens, and enable log export/retention to prevent further tampering. 3) Hunt: reconstruct the deleted jobs' query scope from surviving ApiEvent/BulkApi telemetry and check for secret-hunting SOQL and vendor-token abuse by the same actor.

| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Delete","Abort","Remove")
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend TargetObj = coalesce(ObjectType, tostring(Raw.EntityName), tostring(Raw.ObjectType))
| where TargetObj has_any ("AsyncApexJob","BackgroundOperation","BulkApiJob","BulkApi") or ActionType has "Abort"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, ActionType, ObjectType, ObjectName, ObjectId
| order by Timestamp desc

Unauthenticated Salesforce Aura/GraphQL guest scraping past 2,000-record limit AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated guest-user hits to the Salesforce Experience Cloud Aura endpoint (/s/sfsites/aura) using cursor-based GraphQL pagination and modified AuraInspector tooling to pull records beyond the 2,000-row cap. Best expressed on WAF/proxy web logs fronting the Experience Cloud site. Rationale: Uses the concrete guest-access endpoint /s/sfsites/aura and the named AuraInspector tooling from the article and GTIG's AuraInspector write-up; cursor-paginated volume past the 2,000-record cap gives a clean threshold on scraping vs. normal public-site browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/auditing-salesforce-aura-data-exposure • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/salesforce-graphql-guest-user-exploit-key-actions-to-take • https://appomni.com/ao-labs/salesforce-graphql-exploit-explained/
ATT&CKT1213 T1530 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate security team running the original Mandiant AuraInspector to audit their own guest exposure
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring hitting the Experience Cloud site repeatedly
  • SEO crawler or archiver paginating public community content
  • Load test against the Experience Cloud site
  • Vendor security scan authorized against the public site
Suppression filter
| where not (UA has "AuraInspector" and SourceIP in ("<internal-security-scanner-ip>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP/ASN is external and unauthenticated, and check whether the guest profile has 'API Enabled' plus over-broad object/field permissions on the queried objects. 2) Contain: remove 'API Enabled' from the guest user profile, tighten guest object/field-level security and sharing rules, and block the scraping IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: quantify which objects/records were exposed via the Aura/GraphQL responses, review other Experience Cloud sites in the org for the same misconfig, and search for the same UA/IP across tenants.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| extend Raw = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend Uri = tostring(coalesce(Raw.Uri, Raw.RequestUrl, Raw.Page))
| where Uri has "/s/sfsites/aura" or Uri has "aura?r="
| where AccountType has_any ("Guest","Anonymous","Unauthenticated") or UserAgent has "AuraInspector"
| summarize Requests = count(), Uris = dcount(Uri), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by IPAddress, UserAgent, CountryCode, ISP
| where Requests > 200   // cursor-paginated scraping (2000-row pages) far exceeds human browsing of a public site
| order by Requests desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/s/sfsites/aura" or RequestURL has "aura?r="
| extend UA = tostring(RequestClientApplication)
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctUris = dcount(RequestURL), Methods = make_set(RequestMethod, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, UA, DestinationHostName
| where Requests > 200   // high-volume cursor pagination of the guest Aura endpoint
   or UA has "AuraInspector"
| order by Requests desc
title: Salesforce guest Aura endpoint access via AuraInspector tooling
id: a91c6d30-4f28-4b17-8e63-2d5f0c7a9b81
description: Detects requests to the Salesforce Experience Cloud guest Aura endpoint (/s/sfsites/aura) from AuraInspector or scripted user agents, used to scrape CRM records past the 2000-row GraphQL limit.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/auditing-salesforce-aura-data-exposure
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1213
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1530
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/s/sfsites/aura'
  selection_tool:
    cs-user-agent|contains:
      - 'AuraInspector'
      - 'python-requests'
      - 'aiohttp'
      - 'Go-http-client'
  condition: selection_path and selection_tool
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.uri_path) as paths from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/s/sfsites/aura*" OR Web.uri_path="*/s/sfsites/aura*") by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=1h 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` 
| where count > 200 
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.uri_path) as paths from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/s/sfsites/aura*" OR Web.uri_path="*/s/sfsites/aura*") by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=1h 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` 
| where count > 200 
| sort - count
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

logsource:

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kimai authenticated session activity with no preceding form-login POST (forged remember-me cookie) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Kimai (Symfony) authenticated access to admin/API/user routes from a source IP that never submitted a POST to the login form in the lookback window. CVE-2026-52824 lets an attacker with the publicly-known default APP_SECRET forge the KIMAI_REMEMBER cookie and be silently auto-authenticated, so the account 'logs in' without any credential submission crossing the wire. Rationale: Uses Kimai's KIMAI_REMEMBER remember-me cookie name and Symfony's form-login POST as the two anchors from the article; the anti-join (authenticated route access from an IP that never POSTed to login) is the observable footprint of a forged remember-me cookie since Symfony auto-authenticates without a credential exchange. Cross-checked GitLab advisory and Symfony login docs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/kimai/kimai/CVE-2026-52824/ • https://symfony.com/doc/current/security/login_link.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1550.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'remember me' users whose original POST /login happened before the lookback window began
  • SSO / reverse-proxy that terminates auth upstream and forwards without a Kimai form POST
  • Corporate NAT egress where one IP both logs in and is reused by an automation account
  • Health-check / monitoring probes hitting /api with a stored service session
  • Load balancer or CDN rewriting the client source IP so the login POST and the app request appear on different IPs
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and UserAgent !has "kube-probe" and CIp !in (dynamic(["<corporate-egress-not-needed:leave-empty-or-populate-org-CIDRs-in-loginIPs-let>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CIp's full request timeline; confirm the first authenticated request truly has no prior POST to /login and inspect whether Cookie carried KIMAI_REMEMBER but never a fresh PHPSESSID handshake. Identify which Kimai account (CsUsername) the session maps to and whether it is super_admin. 2) Contain: rotate APP_SECRET immediately (invalidates all forged cookies/links), force-logout all sessions, and require password reset + enable 2FA on privileged accounts. 3) Hunt: check whether the same IP/UA hit login-link URLs (hash/expires/user params) or created users, changed rates, or exported timesheets; confirm the instance was on Kimai < 2.58.0 with the default secret.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let loginIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where CsMethod == "POST" and CsUriStem has "login"   // Kimai/Symfony form-login check route
    | distinct CIp;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where CsUriStem has_any ("/admin/", "/api/", "/user")   // authenticated Kimai surfaces
| where ScStatus >= 200 and ScStatus < 400
| where CsUsername != "" or Cookie has "KIMAI_REMEMBER"    // session was authenticated
| where CIp !in (loginIPs)                                 // but no form login ever seen from this IP
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20) by CIp, UserAgent, CsUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc

| sort - lastTime
Kimai forged Symfony login-link request (user+expires+hash signed URL) to super_admin AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound GET requests whose query string carries the Symfony passwordless login-link signature triad — user, expires and hash. With the default APP_SECRET (CVE-2026-52824) an unauthenticated attacker can mint valid login links for any account, so a burst of these signed URLs (especially targeting the id=1/super_admin identifier) from external IPs is a direct forgery indicator. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit 'LoginLink signatures' forgery vector and the Symfony-documented login-link parameter triad (user/expires/hash); matching all three tokens in the query string is a distinctive single-event signature that fires even without knowing Kimai's exact check-route path. Cross-checked Symfony login-link docs and the GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/kimai/kimai/CVE-2026-52824/ • https://symfony.com/doc/current/security/login_link.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organisation legitimately uses Symfony/Kimai passwordless login links for real users
  • Password-reset or email-verification links that reuse a similar signed-URL shape
  • Security scanners (Burp/ZAP) fuzzing query parameters named user/expires/hash
  • Uptime monitors replaying a captured login-link URL
  • Other Symfony apps behind the same proxy emitting UriSigner-style links
Suppression filter
| where CsUriStem !has "password-reset" and UserAgent !has_any ("ZAP", "Burp", "Nuclei", "masscan")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract TargetUser from CsUriQuery; determine whether the value corresponds to the id=1/super_admin username and whether the request returned 200/302 (link accepted). Check the source IP's geo/ASN and whether it is external. 2) Contain: if the login link was accepted, rotate APP_SECRET (invalidates every forged link), kill active sessions, reset the targeted account's password and enforce 2FA. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same CIp/UA for subsequent authenticated admin/API activity and for KIMAI_REMEMBER-cookie sessions; verify the deployment ran the default APP_SECRET on Kimai < 2.58.0.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CsMethod == "GET"
| where CsUriQuery has "hash=" and CsUriQuery has "expires=" and CsUriQuery has "user="   // Symfony login-link signed URL triad
| extend TargetUser = extract(@"(?i)user=([^&]+)", 1, CsUriQuery)
| project TimeGenerated, CIp, UserAgent, CsUriStem, CsUriQuery, TargetUser, ScStatus, CsUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud npm worm payload/workflow file drop (bundle.js, setup_bun.js, shai-hulud-workflow.yml) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud supply-chain worm dropping its self-replicating payload and CI persistence file onto developer machines during npm install. Fires on the confirmed malicious bundle.js SHA256 or the distinctive worm filenames written by node/npm. Rationale: Uses the second-source-confirmed Shai-Hulud bundle.js SHA256 (46faab8a...) and the campaign's distinctive filenames (shai-hulud-workflow.yml, setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) named across Unit42/Wiz/Datadog write-ups of the article's flagship campaign; hash+filename anchors make this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately named a file bundle.js under a non-malicious .github/workflows path (rare — that dir holds YAML, not JS)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a Shai-Hulud sample in a sandbox/analysis VM
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies of the payload re-triggering the file-write event from the quarantine folder
  • Threat-intel/IR team staging IOC files named setup_bun.js for tabletop or purple-team exercises
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Windows Defender\", @"\Quarantine\") or DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName node.exe/npm) and the folder — a real hit is bundle.js/setup_bun.js executed during an npm/bun install in a repo working dir. Check the file SHA256 against 46faab8a... 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, revoke and rotate all npm tokens, GitHub PATs, and cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure) keys used from it; check GitHub for a newly-created public repo named 'Shai-Hulud' and any 'shai-hulud-workflow.yml' pushed to your repos. 3) HUNT: Pivot to outbound connections to webhook.site from the same host, enumerate every package version installed in the last 24h, and scope other developers who installed the same dependency.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (SHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09")
     or FileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
     or (FileName =~ "bundle.js" and FolderPath has @"\.github\workflows")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileSHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09")
     or TargetFileName in~ ("shai-hulud-workflow.yml","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
     or (TargetFileName =~ "bundle.js" and TargetFilePath has @"\.github\workflows")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud credential exfiltration: node/npm outbound to webhook.site AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Shai-Hulud worm's credential exfiltration stage where the postinstall payload beacons harvested npm/GitHub/cloud tokens to the hardcoded webhook.site drop (bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7). Pairs the webhook.site destination with a node/npm/bun/git initiating process to cut the FP from legit webhook testing. Rationale: Anchors on the second-source-confirmed hardcoded exfil host webhook.site (Shai-Hulud endpoint bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) but requires a node/npm/bun/git initiating process so it fires on postinstall exfil, not a developer manually testing a webhook in a browser. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1567 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using webhook.site to test an outbound webhook from a Node app during development
  • CI runner (node/git) hitting a webhook.site URL configured in a test suite or integration fixture
  • QA automation posting to webhook.site as a capture endpoint
  • Internal tooling that uses webhook.site free-tier bins for prototyping event delivery
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","postinstall","ci","exec") and not (DeviceName has_any ("build-agent","ci-runner") and InitiatingProcessAccountName has "jenkins")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full RemoteUrl/DNS path — a real hit posts to a webhook.site UUID bin (campaign default bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7) shortly after an npm/bun install; check InitiatingProcessCommandLine for a package install and correlate with a bundle.js/setup_bun.js write in the last hour. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, immediately rotate npm tokens, GitHub PATs, and AWS/GCP/Azure keys from that machine, and block webhook.site at egress. 3) HUNT: Search GitHub audit for a new public 'Shai-Hulud' repo or 'shai-hulud-workflow.yml' commits under affected users, and scope every other host that installed the same package version.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "webhook.site"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","bun.exe","git.exe","curl.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "webhook.site"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or SHA1 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or SHA1 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a") or MD5 in~ ("46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09", "62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0", "f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068", "cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd", "a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Defending SaaS-based applications against ShinyHunters OAuth abuse

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-13 15 use cases 9 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified threat actor activity with overlapping tradecraft commonly associated with ShinyHunters, including voice phishing (vishing), supply-chain compromise, and misconfigured guest access targeting SaaS-based applications. The post Defending SaaS-based applications against ShinyHunters OAuth abuse appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] First-seen Salesforce Connected App performing bulk API / report export (fake Data Loader) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Salesforce Connected App API activity from ShinyHunters integration-abuse IPs · [LLM] Anomalous Salesforce ReportExport volume — bulk CRM exfiltration · [LLM] Guest-user Aura/GraphQL mass data retrieval from ShinyHunters IOC IP · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Salesforce Connected App API activity from ShinyHunters integration-abuse IPs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts Salesforce API/CRM query activity attributed to a Connected App originating from the specific source IPs Microsoft tied to ShinyHunters/UNC6395 abuse of trusted OAuth integrations (Salesloft Drift, Gainsight, Klue). Because the actors ride sanctioned OAuth tokens, IP is the highest-fidelity anchor available on this telemetry. Rationale: Anchors on the five Microsoft-published IOC IPs (article Table 2; 138.226.246.94 is explicitly the Klue integration performing CRM API queries) scoped to Salesforce API/Connected-App activity — a fixed IP set on SaaS API telemetry is an alerting-grade match with near-zero legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-maps-year-long-shinyhunters.html
ATT&CKT1199 T1550.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate integration vendor (Klue/Gainsight) re-uses one of these IPs post-remediation for sanctioned traffic
  • Corporate egress NAT coincidentally shares an IP block with a listed address
  • Threat-intel enrichment jobs or a SOC replay hitting the Salesforce API from a sinkholed IP
  • Security researcher / IR team validating the IOC against the tenant
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all CloudAppEvents for the matched IP, note the ConnectedAppId and AccountDisplayName acting on its behalf, and confirm whether the app is an approved Salesloft/Gainsight/Klue integration. 2) Contain: in Salesforce, revoke the Connected App's OAuth tokens and block the source IP at the org login-IP-range/Connected-App policy; rotate the integration's connection secret. 3) Hunt: enumerate every ReportExport/BulkApi call by that ConnectedAppId, pivot to other tenants/users the same app touched, and search for the remaining four IOC IPs and any credentials exposed in exported records.

First-seen Salesforce Connected App performing bulk API / report export (fake Data Loader) AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces a Connected App ID that has never been observed in the tenant baseline suddenly issuing API calls or report exports — the pattern left by ShinyHunters' vishing-driven OAuth consent to a malicious app disguised as the legitimate Salesforce Data Loader. Catches consent-phishing even when the source IP is not a known IOC. Rationale: Uses the article's own ConnectedAppId extraction (RawEventData.CONNECTED_APP_ID / ConnectedAppId, code Block 1) but replaces the non-schema UncommonForUser flag with a 30-day first-seen anti-join — a newly-consented app doing bulk API/export is exactly the malicious 'Data Loader' behaviour Microsoft describes. Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental

DeviceNetworkEvents
